On the Stability of Solitary Wave Solutions for a Generalized Fractional Benjamin-Bona-Mahony Equation

Goksu Oruc G. OrucIstanbul Technical University, Department of Mathematics, Maslak, Istanbul, Turkey. Email address: topkarci@itu.edu.tr , Fábio Natali F. NataliDepartment of Mathematics, State University of Maringá, Maringá, PR, Brazil. Email address: fmanatali@uem.br , Handan Borluk H. BorlukOzyegin University, Department of Natural and Mathematical Sciences, Cekmekoy, Istanbul, Turkey. Email address: handan.borluk@ozyegin.edu.tr and Gulcin M. Muslu G. M. MusluIstanbul Technical University, Department of Mathematics, Maslak, Istanbul, Turkey. Email address: gulcin@itu.edu.tr
Abstract.

In this paper we establish a rigorous spectral stability analysis for solitary waves associated to a generalized fractional Benjamin-Bona-Mahony type equation. Besides the well known smooth and positive solitary wave with large wave speed, we present the existence of smooth negative solitary waves having small wave speed. The spectral stability is then determined by analysing the behaviour of the associated linearized operator around the wave restricted to the orthogonal of the tangent space related to the momentum at the solitary wave. Since the analytical solution is not known, we generate the negative solitary waves numerically by using Petviashvili method. We also present some numerical experiments to observe the stability properties of solitary waves for various values of the order of nonlinearity and fractional derivative. Some remarks concerning the orbital stability are also celebrated.

Key words and phrases: 
Generalized Fractional Benjamin-Bona-Mahony equation, Orbital Stability, Spectral Instability, Solitary Waves.
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
76B25, 35Q51, 35Q53.

1. Introduction

In this paper we consider the stability properties of the solitary wave solutions for the generalized fractional Benjamin-Bona-Mahony (gfBBM) equation given by

(1.1) ut+ux+12​(up+1)x+34​Dα​ux+54​Dα​ut=0.u_{t}+u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}(u^{p+1})_{x}+\frac{3}{4}D^{\alpha}u_{x}+\frac{5}{4}D^{\alpha}u_{t}=0.

Here pp is an integer and the operator Dα=(−∂x2)α2D^{\alpha}=(-\partial_{x}^{2})^{\frac{\alpha}{2}} denotes the Riesz potential of order −α-\alpha, for any α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}. The operator DαD^{\alpha} is defined via Fourier transform by

Dα​q^​(ξ)=|ξ|α​q^​(ξ),\widehat{D^{\alpha}q}(\xi)=|\xi|^{\alpha}\hat{q}(\xi),

where q^\hat{q} is the Fourier transform in L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) of the function qq. The gfBBM equation admits the following conserved quantities

(1.2) I⁡(u)\displaystyle I(u) =\displaystyle= ∫−∞+∞u​𝑑x,\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}udx,
(1.3) F⁡(u)\displaystyle F(u) =\displaystyle= 12​∫−∞+∞(u2+54​|Dα2​u|2)​𝑑x,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\left(u^{2}+\frac{5}{4}|D^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}u|^{2}\right)dx,
(1.4) H⁡(u)\displaystyle H(u) =\displaystyle= −12∫−∞∞(u2+up+2p+2+34|Dα2u|2)dx.\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left({u^{2}}+\frac{u^{p+2}}{p+2}+\frac{3}{4}|D^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}u|^{2}\right)dx.

Equation (1.1) is derived to model the propagation of small amplitude long unidirectional waves in a non-locally and non-linearly elastic medium [9, 10].
The Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation

ut+ux+u​ux+ux​x​x=0u_{t}+u_{x}+uu_{x}+u_{xxx}=0

is one of the most celebrated equations in water wave theory. Due to the shortcomings of the KdV equation, new approximate models are developed for water waves. A well-known alternative model is the Benjamin-Bona-Mahony (BBM) equation

ut+ux+u​ux−ux​x​t=0u_{t}+u_{x}+uu_{x}-u_{xxt}=0

derived in [5]. The dispersion relation for the linear BBM equation is the Padé (0,2)-approximation to the full dispersion relation. To provide a better approximation of the dispersion relation for the small wave numbers, the Padé (2,2)-approximation is used to derive the equation,

(1.5) ut+ux+u​ux−910​ux​x​x−1910​ux​x​t=0,u_{t}+u_{x}+uu_{x}-\frac{9}{10}u_{xxx}-\frac{19}{10}u_{xxt}=0,

which involves both linear terms for the KdV and BBM equations [12]. The same equation is also established for Boussinesq-like equations with improved frequency dispersion to model unidirectional surface water waves [7]. The authors in [25] showed numerically that the solutions of the equation (1.5) provides a better approximation to the solutions of the full Euler equations than either the KdV or BBM equations.

The effects of the relation between the nonlinearity and the dispersion on the dynamics of solutions has been the focus of many studies. For this aim, the fractional equations are widely studied in recent years [22, 23, 20, 29, 8, 27, 3]. The fractional forms of the KdV equation and the BBM equation are given as the fractional KdV (fKdV) equation

(1.6) ut+ux+up​ux−Dα​ux=0,u_{t}+u_{x}+u^{p}u_{x}-D^{\alpha}u_{x}=0,

and fractional BBM (fBBM) equation

(1.7) ut+ux+up​ux+Dα​ut=0,u_{t}+u_{x}+u^{p}u_{x}+D^{\alpha}u_{t}=0,

respectively. The gfBBM equation involves the fractional terms of both the fKdV and fBBM equations. The efficiency of the equation (1.5) makes the gfBBM equation more interesting. This paper gives an insight into the dynamics of the solutions for the gfBBM equation.

The local well-posedness of Cauchy problem for both equations (1.6)(\ref{fkdv}) and (1.7)(\ref{fbbm}) is investigated in [1] and [22]. In the case p=1p=1, the missing uniqueness result is recovered for the equation (1.7)(\ref{fbbm}) in [15]. The existence and orbital stability of positive solitary wave solutions with the form u⁡(x,t)=Qc​(x−c​t)u(x,t)=Q_{c}(x-ct) for both fKdV and fBBM equations are discussed in [23] and [29] using variational methods. The case α=2\alpha=2 deserves to be highlighted as it corresponds to the classical KdV and BBM equations. Concerning the equation (1.6)(\ref{fkdv}), the authors in [6] have exhibited a scenario for the orbital stability of solitary waves with sech-type profile for c>0c>0. In fact, orbital stability in the energy space H1​(ℝ)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}) occurs for 1≤p<41\leq p<4 and orbital instability is determined for p>4p>4. The case p=4p=4 is well known as L2−L^{2}-critical case and orbital instability results have been established in [11] and [24]. For the equation (1.7)(\ref{fbbm}) and c>1c>1, we have a similar scenario. Indeed, using suitable adaptations of the approach in [6], the authors in [30] have established the orbital stability of solitary waves with s​e​c​h−sech-profile for the case 1≤p≤41\leq p\leq 4. For the case p>4p>4, the solitary waves are orbitally unstable for 1<c<c01<c<c_{0} and orbitally stable for c>c0c>c_{0}. Here, c0c_{0} is a critical value depending on pp.

The existence, uniqueness and spectral stability of periodic waves for the fKdV and the fBBM equations are also studied in [3] and [27]. The stability behaviour of the solutions changes drastically for the fKdV and the fBBM equations. To illustrate in the case p=1p=1, it has been shown that the solitary wave solutions of the fKdV equation are orbitally stable for c>0c>0 when α∈(12,2)\alpha\in(\frac{1}{2},2) and spectrally unstable when α∈(13,12)\alpha\in(\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{2}). The solitary wave solutions of the fBBM equation are orbitally stable when c>1c>1 and α∈[12,2)\alpha\in[\frac{1}{2},2) or when c>c1>1c>c_{1}>1 and α∈(13,12)\alpha\in(\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{2}) (c1c_{1} is also a critical value depending on α\alpha). The solutions are spectrally unstable when α∈(13,12)\alpha\in(\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{2}) and 1<c<c11<c<c_{1}. Therefore the stability problem for the solitary wave solutions of the gfBBM equation is crucial since the equation involves the fractional terms of both the fKdV and the fBBM equations.

An important feature of the gfBBM equation is that it admits negative solitary wave solutions. In this study, we prove the existence of negative solitary wave solutions for small wave speed and odd values of the order of nonlinearity pp. To the best of our knowledge, the existence of negative solitary wave has never been investigated for the fKdV and fBBM equations when α∈(0,2)\alpha\in(0,2). The negative solitary waves first appeared in [21] for a regularized long wave model in water waves. For the BBM equation, α=2\alpha=2 in the equation (1.7)(\ref{fbbm}), the authors in [16] established the existence of negative solitary waves when c<0c<0 and pp odd. Using arguments of symmetry and the existence of positive solutions QcQ_{c} with c>1c>1 (see [30]), it is possible to prove that the case pp even also admits negative solitary waves of the form −Qc-Q_{c} for c>1c>1. The orbital stability of negative solitary waves has been also treated in [16] (see [17] for a complementary result). For p≥1p\geq 1 odd and c<0c<0, there exists a critical value c2<0c_{2}<0 such that the solitary wave is orbitally unstable for c2<c<0c_{2}<c<0 and orbitally stable for c<c2c<c_{2}. For p>2p>2 even, we have a similar scenario as in the case of positive and solitary waves since the negative solution in this case is given by −Qc-Q_{c}, where QcQ_{c} is the positive solution for c>1c>1.

One of the main properties which guarantee the existence of solitary waves of the form u⁡(x,t)=Qc​(x−c​t)u(x,t)=Q_{c}(x-ct) is the presence of translation symmetry at the spatial variable associated to the equation (1.1)(\ref{gfBBM}). In fact, if u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) is a solution for (1.1)(\ref{gfBBM}), so that u⁡(x+y,t)u(x+y,t) is also a solution of the same equation for all y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R}. An important question arises with the presence of the translation symmetry: if the initial value u0u_{0} of the associated Cauchy problem for the equation (1.1)(\ref{gfBBM}) is close to the solitary wave QcQ_{c}, can we conclude that the corresponding evolution u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) is close to the orbit generated by translations associated to QcQ_{c}? Roughly speaking, we have defined the notion of orbital stability for the solitary wave QcQ_{c}. More precisely, the formal definition for this concept is given as follows:

Definition 1.1.

Let QcQ_{c} be a traveling wave solution for (1.1). We say that QcQ_{c} is orbitally stable in Hα2​(ℝ)H^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}(\mathbb{R}) provided that, given ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists a δ>0\delta>0 with the following property: if u0∈Hα2​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}(\mathbb{R}) satisfies ‖u0−Qc‖Hα2<δ\|u_{0}-Q_{c}\|_{H^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}}<\delta, then the local solution, u⁡(t)u(t), defined in some interval [0,T′)[0,T^{\prime}) of (1.1) with initial condition u0u_{0} can be continued for a solution in 0≤t<+∞0\leq t<+\infty and satisfies

supt∈(0,+∞)infx0∈ℝ||u(⋅,t)−Qc(⋅−x0)||Hα2<ε.\sup_{t\in(0,+\infty)}\inf_{x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}}||u(\cdot,t)-Q_{c}(\cdot-x_{0})||_{H^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}}<\varepsilon.

Otherwise, we say that QcQ_{c} is orbitally unstable in Hα2​(ℝ)H^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}(\mathbb{R}).

In the current study, we discuss the orbital stability of solitary wave solutions of the gfBBM equation in the case of quadratic and cubic non-linearities, that is, p=1p=1 and p=2p=2, respectively. To illustrate the reason only in the case p=1p=1, we can mention that our notion of orbital stability contemplates only local solutions and we can show such property using the approach in Grillakis, Shatah and Strauss [14] for all c>1c>1 when 12≤α≤2\frac{1}{2}\leq\alpha\leq 2 and for c>c1>1c>c_{1}>1 with c1=9​α+2+2​3​α−115​αc_{1}=\frac{9\alpha+2+\sqrt{2}\sqrt{3\alpha-1}}{15\alpha} when 13<α<12\frac{1}{3}<\alpha<\frac{1}{2}. We also have orbital stability result for c2<c<3/5c_{2}<c<3/5 with c2=9​α+2−2​3​α−115​αc_{2}=\frac{9\alpha+2-\sqrt{2}\sqrt{3\alpha-1}}{15\alpha} when 1≤α≤21\leq\alpha\leq 2.

In order to fill out the lack of stability results we present a spectral (in)stability for the solitary wave QcQ_{c}. Equation (1.1) can be rewritten in the Hamiltonian form as

(1.8) ut=J​H′​(u),u_{t}=JH^{\prime}(u),

where J=(I+54Dα)−1∂xJ=(I+\frac{5}{4}D^{\alpha})^{-1}\partial_{x} is a skew-symmetric operator and HH denotes the Hamiltonian of the corresponding equation given by (1.4). It is well known that the abstract theory of orbital instability in [14] can not be applied since JJ present in the equation (1.8)(\ref{H-form}) is not onto. We also show that the solitary wave solution is spectrally stable in the same region of orbital stability.

The paper is organized as follows: In Section 2 we give the global well-posedness result for the Cauchy problem associated with the gfBBM equation. Section 3 is devoted to the existence of negative solitary waves. We investigate the orbital and spectral stabilities of solitary wave solutions in Section 4. In Section 5, we present some numerical experiments to investigate the stability of the solutions and to understand the behaviour of negative travelling wave solutions.

Throughout this study, CC denotes the generic constant.

2. Global Solutions of the Cauchy Problem for the gfBBM Equation

The local existence of solutions for the Cauchy problem

(2.1) ut+ux+12​(up+1)x+34​Dα​ux+54​Dα​ut=0,\displaystyle u_{t}+u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}(u^{p+1})_{x}+\frac{3}{4}D^{\alpha}u_{x}+\frac{5}{4}D^{\alpha}u_{t}=0,
(2.2) u​(x,0)=u0​(x)\displaystyle u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)

in the case 0<α<10<\alpha<1 is proved by introducing the following regularization

(2.3) utϵ+uxϵ+12​[(uϵ)p+1]x+34​Dα​uxϵ+54​Dα​utϵ−ϵ​ux​xϵ=0,\displaystyle u_{t}^{\epsilon}+u_{x}^{\epsilon}+\frac{1}{2}[(u^{\epsilon})^{p+1}]_{x}+\frac{3}{4}D^{\alpha}u_{x}^{\epsilon}+\frac{5}{4}D^{\alpha}u_{t}^{\epsilon}-\epsilon u^{\epsilon}_{xx}=0,
(2.4) uϵ​(x,0)=u0ϵ​(x).\displaystyle u^{\epsilon}(x,0)=u_{0}^{\epsilon}(x).

(2.1)-(2.2) in C⁡([0,T′),Hr​(ℝ))C([0,T^{\prime}),H^{r}(\mathbb{R})) as ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0.

Now, we consider the case α>1\alpha>1. The Cauchy problem (2.1)-(2.2) is rewritten as

(2.5) ut+(I+34​Dα)​(I+54​Dα)−1​ux=−12​(I+54​Dα)−1​(up+1)x,\displaystyle u_{t}+({I+\displaystyle\frac{3}{4}D^{\alpha}})({I+\displaystyle\frac{5}{4}D^{\alpha}})^{-1}u_{x}=-\frac{1}{2}(I+\displaystyle\frac{5}{4}D^{\alpha})^{-1}(u^{p+1})_{x},

3. Existence of Negative Solitary Wave Solutions

A solitary wave solution associated to (1.1)(\ref{gfBBM}) is a smooth solution of the form u​(x,t)=Qc​(ξ)u(x,t)=Q_{c}(\xi), ξ=x−c​t\xi=x-ct with wave speed c>0c>0 and satisfying the decay property lim|ξ|→∞Qc(n)​(ξ)=0\displaystyle{\lim_{|\xi|\rightarrow\infty}Q_{c}^{(n)}(\xi)=0}, n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. Using this ansatz on (1.1) we obtain,

(3.1) −c​Qc′+Qc′+12​(Qcp+1)′−54​c​Dα​Qc′+34​Dα​Qc′=0.-cQ_{c}^{\prime}+Q_{c}^{\prime}+\frac{1}{2}(Q_{c}^{p+1})^{\prime}-\frac{5}{4}cD^{\alpha}Q_{c}^{\prime}+\frac{3}{4}D^{\alpha}Q_{c}^{\prime}=0.

Integrating on ℝ\mathbb{R}, the above equation reduces to the following ODE

(3.2) (54​c−34)​Dα​Qc+(c−1)​Qc−12​Qcp+1=0.(\frac{5}{4}c-\frac{3}{4})D^{\alpha}Q_{c}+(c-1)Q_{c}-\frac{1}{2}Q_{c}^{p+1}=0.

In [28], it is stated that the equation (1.1) has nontrivial solutions when c<3/5c<3/5 or c>1c>1 and α>p/(p+2)\alpha>p/(p+2). The existence and uniqueness of positive solitary waves Qc∈Hα2​(ℝ)Q_{c}\in H^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}(\mathbb{R}) for c>1c>1 and α>pp+2\alpha>\frac{p}{p+2} are also proved in [28]. We note that even though only the case 0<α<10<\alpha<1 is considered in [28], the theory in [13] gives the existence of positive solitary waves for 0<α<20<\alpha<2.

Now we discuss the existence of negative solitary wave solutions. According to the Pohozaev type identity

(3.3) (54​c−34)​∫ℝ|Dα2​Qc|2​𝑑x+(c−1)​∫ℝQc2​𝑑x=12​∫ℝQcp+2​𝑑x\big(\frac{5}{4}c-\frac{3}{4}\big)\int_{\mathbb{{R}}}|D^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}Q_{c}|^{2}dx+(c-1)\int_{\mathbb{{R}}}Q_{c}^{2}dx=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{{R}}}Q_{c}^{p+2}dx

given in [28], it is possible to say that the identity is satisfied for a negative QcQ_{c} when c<3/5c<3/5 and pp is odd. To show the existence of such waves we use the result of [13]. Setting Qc=−RcQ_{c}=-R_{c} where Rc>0R_{c}>0 the equation (3.2) becomes

(3.4) (34−54​c)​Dα​Rc+(1−c)​Rc−12​Rcp+1=0.(\frac{3}{4}-\frac{5}{4}c)D^{\alpha}R_{c}+(1-c)R_{c}-\frac{1}{2}R_{c}^{p+1}=0.

A scaling argument as Rc​(ξ)=(2​(1−c))1/p​Q​((4​(c−1)5​c−3)1/α​ξ)R_{c}(\xi)=(2(1-c))^{1/p}Q\left(\left(\frac{4(c-1)}{5c-3}\right)^{1/\alpha}\xi\right) converts (3.4) into the equation

(3.5) Dα​Q+Q−Qp+1=0.D^{\alpha}Q+Q-Q^{p+1}=0.

The existence and uniqueness of an even and positive solution Q∈Hα/2​(ℝ)Q\in H^{\alpha/2}(\mathbb{R}) for (3.5) has been determined in [13] for 0<α<20<\alpha<2 and 0<p<pm​a​x0<p<p_{max}. Here, pmaxp_{\max} is the critical exponent given by

(3.6) pmax​(α)={2​α1−α,for​0<α<1∞,for​1≤α<2.p_{\max}(\alpha)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}\frac{2\alpha}{1-\alpha},&\mbox{for}~~0<\alpha<1\\ \infty,&\mbox{for}~~1\leq\alpha<2.\end{array}\right.

Therefore, we obtain the existence and uniqueness of a positive even solution RcR_{c} of the equation (3.4) and consequently a negative solution QcQ_{c} of the equation (3.2) when c<3/5c<3/5 and pp is odd for 0<α<20<\alpha<2. In Figure 1, we depict existence of solitary waves for different values of α\alpha and cc with p=1p=1.
For the case of α=2\alpha=2 and p=1p=1 the equation (1.1) has the exact solution

(3.7) u⁡(x,t)=3​(c−1)​sech2​(12​4​(c−1)5​c−3​(x−c​t)).u(x,t)=3({c-1})\mbox{sech}^{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{4(c-1)}{5c-3}}(x-ct)\right).

It is clear that (3.7)(\ref{exact}) agrees with the following statement: the solution is positive when c>1c>1 and it is negative when c<3/5c<3/5.

To finish, we note that if Qc​(x−c​t)>0Q_{c}(x-ct)>0 is a solitary wave solution for the gfBBM equation, then −Qc​(x−c​t)-Q_{c}(x-ct) is also a solution when c>1c>1 and pp is even. However, we do not consider these negative solutions in the current study since the dynamics for the solutions QcQ_{c} and −Qc-Q_{c} are the same.

4. Spectral and Orbital Stability of Solitary Waves

In this section, we study the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves. To obtain a precise definition of spectral stability, we need to add a perturbation vv to the smooth travelling wave QcQ_{c} propagating with the same fixed speed cc of the form u⁡(x,t)=Qc​(x−c​t)+v⁡(x−c​t,t)u(x,t)=Q_{c}(x-ct)+v(x-ct,t) in (1.1)(\ref{gfBBM}). Using that QcQ_{c} satisfies (3.2)(\ref{sw1}) and performing a truncating by the linear terms in vv, we obtain evolution problem

(4.1) vt=J​ℒc​v,v_{t}=J\mathcal{L}_{c}v,

where ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c} is the second order differential linearized operator in the form

(4.2) ℒc=(54​c−34)​Dα+c−1−p+12​Qcp.\mathcal{L}_{c}=\left(\frac{5}{4}c-\frac{3}{4}\right)D^{\alpha}+c-1-\frac{p+1}{2}Q_{c}^{p}.

For λ∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathbb{C}, we consider a growing mode solution of the form v⁡(x,t)=eλ​t​w​(x)v(x,t)=e^{\lambda t}w(x) which yields

(4.3) J​ℒc​w=λ​w.J\mathcal{L}_{c}w=\lambda w.

Denoting the spectrum of J​ℒcJ\mathcal{L}_{c} by σ⁡(J​ℒc)\sigma(J\mathcal{L}_{c}), the spectral stability of the solitary wave QcQ_{c} is defined as follows:

Definition 4.1.

The solitary wave Qc∈H∞​(ℝ)Q_{c}\in H^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) is said to be spectrally stable if σ⁡(J​ℒc)⊂i​ℝ\sigma(J\mathcal{L}_{c})\subset i\mathbb{R} in L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}). Otherwise, that is, if σ⁡(J​ℒc)\sigma(J\mathcal{L}_{c}) in L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) contains a point λ\lambda with R​e​(λ)>0Re(\lambda)>0, the solitary wave QcQ_{c} is said to be spectrally unstable.

Remark 4.1.

Following the arguments quoted in the paragraph below [29, Definition 1.3], we see that (4.1)(\ref{gf-lin}) is linearized equation without forcing or damping terms. This kind of evolution model gives, from (4.3)(\ref{spect-prob}), certain symmetries on the spectrum of σ⁡(ℒc)\sigma(\mathcal{L}_{c}). Indeed, σ⁡(ℒc)\sigma(\mathcal{L}_{c}) will be symmetric with respect to the reflection in the real and imaginary axes so that, it implies that exponentially growing perturbations are always paired with exponentially decaying ones. It is the reason why, in the Definition 4.1, only the spectral parameter λ\lambda satisfying R​e​(λ)>0Re(\lambda)>0 was required.

The spectral stability can be studied for the case of smooth solutions which are global in time. Since ww solves (4.3)(\ref{spect-prob}), a bootstrap argument can be performed to conclude the smoothness of ww, so that the evolution of uu is also smooth as required. Since the solution uu can be considered smooth, we can conclude that the solutions handled in the spectral stability can be considered global in time by Theorem 2.4.
Next, associated to the conservation of mass (1.3), we have the basic orthogonality condition on the perturbation v∈Hα​(ℝ)v\in H^{\alpha}(\mathbb{R}) to the smooth solitary wave Qc∈H∞​(ℝ)Q_{c}\in H^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) given by ⟨F′​(Qc),v⟩=0\langle F^{\prime}(Q_{c}),v\rangle=0 and it is preserved in the time evolution of the linearized equation (4.1). Moreover, it is well known that the spectral stability of the solitary wave QcQ_{c} holds if the linearized operator ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c} is positive on the orthogonal complement of the spanned subspace [F′​(Qc)][F^{\prime}(Q_{c})] in L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}). As it is well-known and assuming that ker⁡(ℒc)=[Qc′]\ker(\mathcal{L}_{c})=[Q_{c}^{\prime}], the positivity property holds if the number of negative eigenvalues of the quantity

(4.4) ℐ:=⟨Qc+54​Dα​Qc,ℒc−1​(Qc+54​Dα​Qc)⟩\mathcal{I}:=\left\langle Q_{c}+\frac{5}{4}D^{\alpha}Q_{c},\mathcal{L}_{c}^{-1}\left(Q_{c}+\frac{5}{4}D^{\alpha}Q_{c}\right)\right\rangle

coincides with the number of negative eigenvalues of ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c} in L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}). Now, since c↦Qcc\mapsto Q_{c} is a smooth curve of solitary waves, it follows by differentiating (3.2) in cc that

(4.5) ℒc​(∂cQc)=−(Qc+54​Dα​Qc).\mathcal{L}_{c}\left(\partial_{c}Q_{c}\right)=-\left(Q_{c}+\frac{5}{4}D^{\alpha}Q_{c}\right).

Hence, the quantity ℐ\mathcal{I} in (4.4) can be rewritten as

(4.6) ℐ=−dd​c​F​(Qc).\mathcal{I}=-\frac{d}{dc}F(Q_{c}).

Let us assume that ker⁡(ℒc)=[Qc′]\ker(\mathcal{L}_{c})=[Q_{c}^{\prime}]. According with [18, Theorem 5.3.1], we can calculate the exact number of negative eigenvalues of ℒc|{F′​(Qc)}⊥\mathcal{L}_{c}|_{\{F^{\prime}(Q_{c})\}^{\bot}} by using the index formula as

(4.7) n⁡(ℒc|{F′​(Qc)}⊥)=n⁡(ℒc)−n⁡(ℐ),n\left(\mathcal{L}_{c}|_{\{F^{\prime}(Q_{c})\}^{\bot}}\right)=n(\mathcal{L}_{c})-n(\mathcal{I}),

where n⁡(𝒜)n(\mathcal{A}) stands the number of negative eigenvalues of a certain linear operator 𝒜\mathcal{A} counting multiplicities. Therefore, if n⁡(ℒc)=n⁡(ℐ)=1n(\mathcal{L}_{c})=n(\mathcal{I})=1 one has the required spectral stability.
To obtain the orbital (nonlinear) stability in the sense of Definition 4.1, we need the following basic result:

Lemma 4.2.

Let Qc∈H∞​(ℝ)Q_{c}\in H^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) be a solitary wave of the equation (3.2). Assume that n⁡(ℒc)=1n(\mathcal{L}_{c})=1 and ker⁡(ℒc)=[Qc′]\ker(\mathcal{L}_{c})=[Q_{c}^{\prime}]. Suppose that Φ=∂cQc∈Hα​(ℝ)\Phi=\partial_{c}Q_{c}\in H^{\alpha}(\mathbb{R}) satisfies ⟨ℒc​Φ,Φ⟩<0\langle\mathcal{L}_{c}\Phi,\Phi\rangle<0 and ⟨ℒc​Φ,v⟩=0\langle\mathcal{L}_{c}\Phi,v\rangle=0, for all v∈Υ0v\in\Upsilon_{0}, where

Υ0={v∈Hα2(ℝ):⟨F′(Qc),v⟩=0},\Upsilon_{0}=\{v\in H^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}(\mathbb{R}):\ \ \langle F^{\prime}(Q_{c}),v\rangle=0\},

where FF is the conserved quantity associated with the equation (1.3). Thus, the solitary wave QcQ_{c} is orbitally stable in Hα2​(ℝ)H^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}(\mathbb{R}). The same result is valid when considering the negative solitary wave RcR_{c} instead of QcQ_{c} and the linearized operator

(4.8) ℒc−=(34−54​c)​Dα+1−c−p+12​Qcp\mathcal{L}_{c}^{-}=\left(\frac{3}{4}-\frac{5}{4}c\right)D^{\alpha}+1-c-\frac{p+1}{2}Q_{c}^{p}

instead of ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c}.

Proof.

The proof of this result is an adaptation of the general orbital stability approach in [14] and [31, Section 2]. For additional references, we can cite [4, Chapter 6] and [26, Section 4] regarding the Korteweg-de Vries/Schrödinger type equations. All mentioned results can be adapted to our model without further problems. Indeed, first we have n⁡(ℒc)=1n(\mathcal{L}_{c})=1 and ker⁡(ℒc)=[Qc′]\ker(\mathcal{L}_{c})=[Q_{c}^{\prime}]. For Φ=∂cQc\Phi=\partial_{c}Q_{c}, one has from (4.5)(\ref{relationphicb}) that ℒc​Φ=−(Qc+54​Dα​Qc)\mathcal{L}_{c}\Phi=-\left(Q_{c}+\frac{5}{4}D^{\alpha}Q_{c}\right) and since ⟨ℒc​Φ,Φ⟩=ℐ=−dd​c​F​(Qc)\langle\mathcal{L}_{c}\Phi,\Phi\rangle=\mathcal{I}=-\frac{d}{dc}F(Q_{c}), we obtain the orbital stability in the sense of Definition 4.1 provided that ℐ<0\mathcal{I}<0 (or equivalently, d′′​(c):=dd​c​F​(Qc)=−ℐ>0d^{\prime\prime}(c):=\frac{d}{dc}F(Q_{c})=-\mathcal{I}>0 as required in [14]). Gathering all informations, we have

(4.9) ⟨ℒc​v,v⟩≥C​‖v‖Hα22,\langle\mathcal{L}_{c}v,v\rangle\geq C||v||_{H^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}}^{2},

for all v∈Υ0∩[Qc′]⊥v\in\Upsilon_{0}\cap[Q_{c}^{\prime}]^{\bot}. The positivity in (4.9)(\ref{positivity}) allows us to conclude the orbital stability in the energy space Hα2​(ℝ)H^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}(\mathbb{R}) since QcQ_{c} is a minimum of the energy functional HH in (1.4)(\ref{hamilton}) for fixed momentum FF in (1.3)(\ref{cq2}). ∎

Remark 4.2.

Using Lemma 4.2 we can affirm, since n⁡(ℒc)=n⁡(ℐ)=1n(\mathcal{L}_{c})=n(\mathcal{I})=1, that the spectral stability implies the orbital stability in our case and vice and versa.

Next, for any k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, if n⁡(ℒc|{F′​(Qc)}⊥)=2​k−1n\left(\mathcal{L}_{c}|_{\{F^{\prime}(Q_{c})\}^{\bot}}\right)=2k-1 we have at least one eigenvalue with positive real part for the operator ∂xℒc\partial_{x}\mathcal{L}_{c} and then, the solitary wave is spectrally unstable (see [29], [19] and references therein).
In order to calculate n⁡(ℒc|{F′​(Qc)}⊥)n\left(\mathcal{L}_{c}|_{\{F^{\prime}(Q_{c})\}^{\bot}}\right) using identity (4.7)(\ref{index-f}), we first need to know the behavior of the non-positive eigenvalues of ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c}. Since the equation (1.1)(\ref{gfBBM}) is invariant under the symmetry of translation, we have at least that Qc′∈ker⁡(ℒc)Q_{c}^{\prime}\in\ker(\mathcal{L}_{c}). However this information is not enough to calculate ℐ\mathcal{I} in (4.4)(\ref{matrix}) since we do not know if ℒc−1​(Qc+54​Dα​Qc)\mathcal{L}_{c}^{-1}\left(Q_{c}+\frac{5}{4}D^{\alpha}Q_{c}\right) is well defined. Next result give us in fact that n⁡(ℒc)=z⁡(ℒc)=1n(\mathcal{L}_{c})=z(\mathcal{L}_{c})=1, where z⁡(ℒc)z(\mathcal{L}_{c}) indicates the dimension of ker⁡(ℒc)\ker(\mathcal{L}_{c}).

Proposition 4.3.

Let α∈(0,2]\alpha\in\left(0,2\right] be fixed and consider 0<p<pm​a​x0<p<p_{max}, with pm​a​xp_{max} defined as in (3.6)(\ref{pcond}). For c>1c>1, the linearized self-adjoint operator ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c} in (4.2) defined in L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}), with the dense domain Hα​(ℝ)H^{\alpha}(\mathbb{R}) satisfies n⁡(ℒc)=z⁡(ℒc)=1n(\mathcal{L}_{c})=z(\mathcal{L}_{c})=1. Moreover, the essential spectrum of ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c} is given by σess(ℒc)=[c−1,+∞)\sigma_{{\rm ess}}(\mathcal{L}_{c})=\left[c-1,+\infty\right).

Proof.

According with [13], let ϕ\phi be the unique solitary wave profile associated with the equation

(4.10) Dα​ϕ+ϕ−ϕp+1=0.D^{\alpha}{\phi}+{\phi}-{\phi}^{p+1}=0.

For θ=(4​(c−1)5​c−3)1/α\theta=\big(\frac{4(c-1)}{5c-3}\big)^{1/{\alpha}}, we have that QcQ_{c} given by

(4.11) Qc​(x)=(2​(c−1))1/p​ϕ​(θ​x)Q_{c}(x)=\big({2(c-1)}\big)^{1/p}{\phi}\big(\theta x\big)

is also the unique solitary wave which solves equation (3.2)(\ref{sw1}).
Next, consider the linearized operator associated with the solitary wave ϕ\phi

(4.12) 𝒫=Dα+1−(p+1)​ϕp.\mathcal{P}=D^{\alpha}+1-(p+1){\phi^{p}}.

According with the arguments in [13], we have that 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a self-adjoint operator defined in L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) with dense domain Hα​(ℝ)H^{\alpha}(\mathbb{R}), the essential spectrum is σe​s​s(𝒫)=[1,+∞)\sigma_{ess}(\mathcal{P})=[1,+\infty) and n⁡(𝒫)=z⁡(𝒫)=1n(\mathcal{P})=z(\mathcal{P})=1. We follow the idea given by [29] in order to relate both operators 𝒫\mathcal{P} and ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c}. In fact, using (4.11)(\ref{transf}) and the dilation operator (Tθ​f)​(x)=f⁡(θ​x),(T_{\theta}f)(x)=f(\theta x), we have that

(4.13) ℒc=(c−1)​Tθ​𝒫​Tθ−1.\mathcal{L}_{c}=(c-1)T_{\theta}\mathcal{P}T_{\theta}^{-1}.

Relation (4.13)(\ref{operators1}) implies that the operators 𝒫\mathcal{P} and ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c} have the same spectral structure, i.e. s​p​e​c​(ℒc)={(c−1)​λ:λ∈s​p​e​c​(𝒫)}spec(\mathcal{L}_{c})=\left\{(c-1)\lambda:\lambda\in spec(\mathcal{P})\right\}. Since both operators are self-adjoint we have that n⁡(ℒc)=z⁡(ℒc)=1n(\mathcal{L}_{c})=z(\mathcal{L}_{c})=1 and σess(ℒc)=[c−1,+∞)\sigma_{{\rm ess}}(\mathcal{L}_{c})=\left[c-1,+\infty\right) as requested. ∎

The spectrum of the linearized operator for the negative solitary wave solutions is given with the following Proposition:

Proposition 4.4.

Let α∈(0,2]\alpha\in\left(0,2\right] be fixed and consider 0<p<pm​a​x0<p<p_{max}, with pp odd and pm​a​xp_{max} defined as in (3.6)(\ref{pcond}). For c<3/5c<3/5, the linearized self-adjoint operator ℒc−\mathcal{L}_{c}^{-} defined in L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}), with the dense domain Hα​(ℝ)H^{\alpha}(\mathbb{R}) satisfies n⁡(ℒc−)=z⁡(ℒc−)=1n(\mathcal{L}_{c}^{-})=z(\mathcal{L}_{c}^{-})=1. Moreover, the essential spectrum of ℒc−\mathcal{L}_{c}^{-} is given by σess(ℒc−)=[1−c,+∞)\sigma_{{\rm ess}}(\mathcal{L}_{c}^{-})=\left[1-c,+\infty\right).

Proof.

We can relate the operator ℒc−\mathcal{L}_{c}^{-} with 𝒫\mathcal{P} with the dilation operator (Tθ​f)​(x)=f⁡(θ​x)(T_{\theta}f)(x)=f(\theta x) where θ=(4​(c−1)5​c−3)1/α\theta=\big(\frac{4(c-1)}{5c-3}\big)^{1/{\alpha}}. We have that

(4.14) ℒc−=(1−c)​Tθ​𝒫​Tθ−1.\mathcal{L}_{c}^{-}=(1-c)T_{\theta}\mathcal{P}T_{\theta}^{-1}.

Relation (4.14)(\ref{operators}) implies that the operators 𝒫\mathcal{P} and ℒc−\mathcal{L}_{c}^{-} have the same spectral structure, i.e. s​p​e​c​(ℒc−)={(1−c)​λ:λ∈s​p​e​c​(𝒫)}spec(\mathcal{L}_{c}^{-})=\left\{(1-c)\lambda:\lambda\in spec(\mathcal{P})\right\}. The rest of the proof is the same as in Proposition 4.3. ∎

We have a convenient result for the quantity ℐ\mathcal{I} given by (4.6)(\ref{matrix-P})

Lemma 4.5.

Let p>0p>0 be fixed and consider α>pp+2\alpha>\frac{p}{p+2}. For c∈(0,35)∪(1,+∞)c\in\left(0,\frac{3}{5}\right)\cup(1,+\infty), we have

ℐ=−dd​c​[(c−1)2/p​(5​c−34​(c−1))1/α​(1+5​p​(c−1)(5​c−3)​(α⁡(p+2)−p))]​‖ϕ‖2.\mathcal{I}=-\frac{d}{dc}\left[(c-1)^{2/p}\bigg(\frac{5c-3}{4(c-1)}\bigg)^{1/{\alpha}}\left(1+\frac{5p(c-1)}{(5c-3)(\alpha(p+2)-p)}\right)\right]\|{\phi}\|^{2}.

Transformation (4.11)(\ref{transf}) applied in the last integral of (4.15)(\ref{pohoz}) enables us to conclude

(4.16) ∫−∞+∞|Qc​(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ=(2​(c−1))2/p​(5​c−3)4​(c−1)1/α​∫−∞+∞|ϕ⁡(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ.\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}|Q_{c}(\xi)|^{2}d\xi=\frac{\big(2(c-1)\big)^{2/p}(5c-3)}{4(c-1)^{1/\alpha}}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}|{\phi}({\xi})|^{2}d{\xi}.

Finally, combining (4.15)(\ref{pohoz}) and (4.16)(\ref{scalL2}) we obtain

ℐ\displaystyle\mathcal{I} =\displaystyle= −dd​cF(Qc)=−12dd​c∫−∞+∞(Qc2+54|Dα2Qc|2)dξ\displaystyle-\frac{d}{dc}F(Q_{c})=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dc}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\left(Q_{c}^{2}+\frac{5}{4}|D^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}Q_{c}|^{2}\right)d\xi
=\displaystyle= −22/p−1​dd​c​[(c−1)2/p​(5​c−34​(c−1))1/α​(1+5​p​(c−1)(5​c−3)​(α⁡(p+2)−p))]​‖ϕ‖2.\displaystyle-2^{2/p-1}\frac{d}{dc}\left[(c-1)^{2/p}\bigg(\frac{5c-3}{4(c-1)}\bigg)^{1/{\alpha}}\left(1+\frac{5p(c-1)}{(5c-3)(\alpha(p+2)-p)}\right)\right]\|{\phi}\|^{2}.

∎

Let p>0p>0 be fixed and consider α>pp+2\alpha>\frac{p}{p+2}. Define 𝒦:(0,35)∪(1,+∞)→ℝ\mathcal{K}:(0,\frac{3}{5})\cup(1,+\infty)\rightarrow\mathbb{R} given by

(4.18) c1=9​α+2+2​3​α−115​α,c2=9​α+2−2​3​α−115​α.c_{1}=\frac{9\alpha+2+\sqrt{2}\sqrt{3\alpha-1}}{15\alpha},~~~~~~~~~c_{2}=\frac{9\alpha+2-\sqrt{2}\sqrt{3\alpha-1}}{15\alpha}.

5. Numerical Results

In this section, we first construct the solitary wave solutions by using Petviashvili’s iteration method. The Petviashvili method for the gfBBM equation is given by

(5.1) Q^n+1​(k)=(Mn)ν2​[(5​c4−34)​|k|α+c−1]​Qnp+1^​(k)\widehat{Q}_{n+1}(k)=\frac{(M_{n})^{\nu}}{2\left[\left(\displaystyle\frac{5c}{4}-\frac{3}{4}\right)|k|^{\alpha}+c-1\right]}\widehat{Q_{n}^{p+1}}(k)

with stabilizing factor

Mn=∫ℝ[(5​c4−34)​|k|α+c−1]​[Q^n​(k)]2​𝑑k12​∫ℝQ^np+1​(k)​Q^n​(k)​𝑑k,M_{n}=\displaystyle\frac{\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left[\left(\displaystyle\frac{5c}{4}-\frac{3}{4}\right)|k|^{\alpha}+c-1\right][\widehat{Q}_{n}(k)]^{2}dk}{\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\displaystyle\widehat{Q}^{p+1}_{n}(k)\widehat{Q}_{n}(k)dk},

for the parameter ν=(p+1)/p\nu=({p+1})/{p}. Here Q^\widehat{Q} denotes the Fourier transform of QcQ_{c}. Then we investigate time evolution of the solutions by using a numerical scheme combining a Fourier pseudo-spectral method for space and a fourth order Runge-Kutta method for the time integration. We assume that u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) has periodic boundary condition u⁡(−L,t)=u⁡(L,t)u(-L,t)=u(L,t) on the truncated domain (x,t)∈[−L,L]×[0,T](x,t)\in[-L,L]\times[0,T]. In the following numerical experiments the space interval and the number of spatial grid points are chosen as [−4096,4096][-4096,4096] and N=218N=2^{18}, respectively. The time step is Δ​t=5×10−4\Delta t=5\times 10^{-4}. We refer [28] for the details of the numerical methods.

We present the negative solitary wave profiles for various values of α\alpha when pp is fixed, and for various values of pp when α\alpha is fixed in Figure 4. In both cases we choose c=0.5c=0.5. In the case of positive solitary waves it is observed in [28] that decreasing the order of fractional derivative and increasing the order of nonlinearity have the same effect on the solutions. However, we do not observe the same behaviour for the negative solitary waves. The amplitude of the negative solitary wave solution increases with the decreasing values of α\alpha whereas the amplitude decreases with the increasing values of pp.

In order to study the stability of solitary wave solutions we choose the initial condition as a perturbation of the solitary wave solution QcQ_{c} obtained by Petviashvili method. Hence the initial condition is of the form

(5.2) u0=γ​Qc​(x)u_{0}=\gamma Q_{c}(x)

where γ\gamma is the perturbation parameter. In the following numerical experiments we choose γ=1.1\gamma=1.1. As a control of the numerical accuracy we make sure that the error |F⁡(t)−F⁡(0)||F(t)-F(0)| in the conserved quantity is less than 10−510^{-5}. We set p=1p=1 for the rest of the numerical experiments.

In Figure 5, we illustrate propagation of the perturbed positive solitary wave solution for α=0.6\alpha=0.6 and c=1.1c=1.1. Analytical results indicate an orbital stability for these values. The numerical result indicates a nonlinear stability which is compatible with theoretical result.

Now, we focus on the interval 13<α<12\frac{1}{3}<\alpha<\frac{1}{2} and c>1c>1. Here we have two subregions: For c>c1c>c_{1}, the solitary waves are orbitally stable whereas, for 1<c<c11<c<c_{1} solitary waves are spectrally unstable. For α=0.45\alpha=0.45 the critical wave speed is c1≈1.04c_{1}\approx 1.04. The evolution of the perturbed stable solution for c=1.1>c1c=1.1>c_{1} is illustrated in Figure 6. Here we observe that the numerical result agrees with the analytical result of the stability.

In Figure 7, we investigate the time evolution of the perturbed solution for α=0.45\alpha=0.45, c=1.035<c1c=1.035<c_{1}. However, we could not observe a visible growth in the solutions as time increases. The analytical results give the spectral instability but we study the nonlinear stability numerically. One of the conditions to obtain that spectral instability implies orbital instability is that the mapping u0↦u⁡(t)u_{0}\mapsto u(t) is smooth. For α∈(13,12)\alpha\in(\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{2}), this is an open problem. Therefore, this observation does not imply a contradiction between the analytical and the numerical results.

The gfBBM equation has negative solitary wave solution when c<35c<\frac{3}{5} and p=1p=1. The propagation of a perturbed negative solitary wave profile for α=0.6\alpha=0.6 and c=0.5c=0.5 is depicted in Figure 8. The amplitude decreases slowly and the small tail like oscillations appear by the time. As in the previous experiment, the numerical result does not imply a nonlinear instability.
